pulls.title: wallet: reject recipient amounts above MAX_MONEY
pulls.body:
`CreateTransaction` checks that recipient amounts aren't negative, but not that they're within `MAX_MONEY`. `CreateTransactionInternal` then sums them into `recipients_sum` (spend.cpp:1100) with no range check, and that sum can overflow.

Easiest way to hit it is `fundrawtransaction` with a raw tx that has two outputs of 2^62 sat. It can also be reached with only valid amounts through `walletcreatefundedpsbt`/`send`/`sendmany` and a few thousand 21M BTC outputs. The "Transaction too large" check only runs after coin selection, so it doesn't stop this. On master the node aborts:

```
Assertion failed: (!m_selected_inputs.empty()), function RecalculateWaste, file coinselection.cpp, line 904.
```

UBSan reports the overflow at spend.cpp:1100 first. With other values the sum wraps to a small positive number instead, and `fundrawtransaction` returns success for a tx with outputs of 46116860184 BTC each.

This checks every amount and the running sum against `MoneyRange` in the existing recipients loop of `CreateTransactionInternal`, before the amount is added to `recipients_sum`, and returns "Transaction output amount must be valid" before coin selection starts. The same check rejects negative amounts, so the separate negative check in `CreateTransaction` is removed. The new `test_outputs_above_max_money` in `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py` covers a single output above MAX_MONEY, two outputs whose sum is above it, a sum that overflows int64, and a negative output. On master the first case returns "Insufficient funds" and the overflow case crashes the node; with the fix all of them get the new error. `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py`, `wallet_send.py`, `wallet_basic.py` and `rpc_psbt.py` pass.

pulls.title: coins,dbwrapper: make point-read and txindex lookup failures fatal
pulls.body:
**Problem:** #34931 made unreadable coin entries fatal, but `CDBWrapper::Read()` still returns `false` for deserialization failures and propagates LevelDB point-read exceptions to callers.
A corrupt txindex point read can consequently fail one RPC while the node continues running.
#35728 reports other txindex lookup failures as errors that callers can also catch while the node continues running.
Chainstate also retains `CCoinsViewErrorCatcher` as a separate view layer to report read errors and abort.

**Fix:** Make LevelDB point-read and typed deserialization failures fatal in `CDBWrapper`, after logging the database path and error and notifying the database owner’s `kernel::Notifications` when supplied.
This includes point-read failures during startup, which now bypass the GUI’s database rebuild offer.
Missing keys still return `false`, database-open failures retain their initialization handling, and iterator behavior remains unchanged.

Pass each owner’s existing notifications at construction for chainstate, the block-index database, optional index databases, and the temporary UTXO database used by `dumptxoutset`.
Remove `TryRead()` and `CCoinsViewErrorCatcher`, keep `HaveCoin()` on the cache view that owns its caching behavior, and mark coin-view lookups `noexcept`.

Make txindex consistency errors and block-file lookup failures fatal through the shared notification path before aborting.
Continue skipping stale entries for unknown blocks and non-active blocks without data.
Direct block reads retain their existing RPC error handling.

pulls.title: wallet: make migration more robust against failures
pulls.body:
This is just me finding a few more edge cases after #34156 and #34176

The goal of the PR is to handle failures in a controlled way. Just so the process can automatically restore the original wallet without requiring user manual intervention.

The covered cases are:

1. During `DoMigration()`: There are methods that can throw exceptions and abruptly abort the process. 
Instead of crashing (GUI) or returning a generic exception, we now will catch and return the error gracefully. This lets the process restore the original wallet automatically.

2. Trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory throws a filesystem exception and skips cleanup.
 Now the process will fail gracefully with a clear error msg, and automatically restore the original wallet.

3. Any failure during `MigrateToSQLite` requires user manual intervention. 
Now the original wallet db will remain untouched, and only be updated once the sqlite db creation fully succeeds.

pulls.title: fuzz: improve ipc fuzz coverage
pulls.body:
This PR follows up on #35118 and continues the IPC fuzzing work proposed in #23015.

The initial ipc fuzz target exercised normal calls through a libmultiprocess client and server. This PR extends the target with

 - Server side assertions that verify arguments arrive unchanged (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35118#issuecomment-4452992198 and https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35118#pullrequestreview-4539477599)
 - A callback call that exercises ipc communication in both directions.
 - Raw capnp requests containing arbitrary transaction and `UniValue` payloads, which are deserialized by a normal libmultiprocess server.
  - Raw capnp responses containing arbitrary transaction and `UniValue` payloads, which are deserialized by a normal libmultiprocess client.

The raw request and response cases allow the fuzz target to exercise deserialization with data that was not first produced by libmultiprocess serialization.

The ipc setup and callback handling closely follow the existing [`libmultiprocess` tests](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/src/ipc/libmultiprocess/test/mp/test/test.cpp), particularly their use of `EventLoop`, `ProxyClient`, `ProxyServer`, two-way pipes, and `initThreadMap`. 

The transaction and UniValue payload cases exercise the serialization hooks defined in [`common-types.h`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/src/ipc/capnp/common-types.h). 

These files may provide useful background when reviewing the changes.

Generated [coverage report](https://enirox001.github.io/coverage/ipc/) after fuzzing the IPC target for a while using the qa-assets corpus.

pulls.title: rpc: Report -rpcwhitelist denials as JSON-RPC errors
pulls.body:
This PR adds two JSON-RPC error codes for requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist`, which until now got an HTTP 403 status with an empty body:

- `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` (-38) is returned for a refused request, with HTTP 200 for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests and 403 for legacy 1.x requests.
- `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` (-39) is returned for the other requests in a refused batch. A refused batch now gets HTTP 200 and an array with an error for each request, and still runs none of them.

**Problem:** `-rpcwhitelist` errors are currently handled differently from other JSON-RPC errors, so clients report them with vague or misleading messages, and for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests the handling does not follow [documented behavior](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/JSON-RPC-interface.md#json-rpc-11-vs-20). Specifically, requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist` get HTTP 403 with an empty body, so the refusal shows up as a generic transport error rather than a specific JSON-RPC error. This is especially a problem for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, which are [supposed to](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/bf1a1f1662427fbf1a43bb951364eface469bdb7) report failed method calls only as JSON-RPC errors, not HTTP errors. The empty reply causes a concrete problem when JSON-RPC requests are sent over IPC instead of HTTP: `bitcoin-cli -ipcconnect` receives only the response body, so a refused call prints a JSON type error instead of a permission error, as described in a [private security review](https://ipcbugs.ofsky.org/audits/ar-56/). Over HTTP, `bitcoin-cli` currently stops at the 403 status and prints only "server returned HTTP error 403" instead of the actual error.

**Solution:** Report whitelist denials like any other failed call: a JSON-RPC error in the body, with the HTTP status the request's version calls for. This brings the behavior in line with the documentation. `bitcoin-cli` then prints the permission error over both HTTP and IPC, with no change to the IPC interface. The fix is a small change to `src/httprpc.cpp` and `src/rpc/protocol.h`, with tests in `rpc_whitelist.py` and `interface_ipc_cli.py`. It comes after two refactoring commits suggested in #36642, which move connection fields out of `JSONRPCRequest` into a new `JSONRPCClient` struct and move the batch loop into a `ProcessBatch()` helper that the refused-batch reply shares. Details in the commit messages.

Compatibility: HTTP clients that send `"jsonrpc": "2.0"` or batches and check for a 403 status need to read the error code instead. Single 1.x requests keep the 403 status, now with an error body.

Open question for review: `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` could be named `RPC_ACCESS_DENIED`, and `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` is documented as batch-specific but would fit any request refused before it runs.

pulls.title: psbt: check sig sighash only if a type is given
pulls.body:
SignPSBTInput() checked existing signatures against an assumed sighash type when neither PSBT_IN_SIGHASH_TYPE nor the sighashtype parameter was given: SIGHASH_DEFAULT for taproot, SIGHASH_ALL otherwise. A PSBT holding a valid 65-byte SIGHASH_ALL taproot signature could then be neither finalized nor signed further.

BIP 174 lets a signer use any sighash type when the field is absent, so the check now runs only when the field or the parameter is given, for every input type. Without the field, RemoveUnnecessaryTransactions() now also looks at the taproot signatures for SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY, so that the non_witness_utxo is kept. A functional test in rpc_psbt.py covers a taproot input signed with ALL, NONE and ALL|ANYONECANPAY without the field. A second commit also keeps the non_witness_utxo of a finalized taproot input, whose signatures are left only in the final witness, and tests it on a key path and a script path.

Fixes #36507.

pulls.title: wallet, migration: Contain all legacy wallet and migration related things in its own subdirectory, namespace, and classes
pulls.body:
Originally, legacy wallet migration was built upon the foundation of being able to load legacy wallets. Now that we no longer support loading legacy wallets, there is no reason to keep any of the legacy wallet loading and migration code in the main wallet objects. Having this co-mingling of never-to-be-changed legacy wallet code and new descriptor wallet code makes it difficult to implement new things into the wallet.

This PR fully separates out all of the legacy wallet related things into a subdirectory `wallet/legacy`, with everything in that directory under a `wallet::legacy_migration` namespace so as to prevent accidental usage outside of legacy wallets. This includes a little bit of duplication with current loading code, but not that much, and we are able to both remove unrelated descriptor wallet loading from the legacy wallet loading, and unrelated legacy wallet loading from normal descriptor wallet loading.

`LegacyWallet` is introduced as a subclass of `CWallet` which contains all of the relevant legacy wallet and migration functions so that `CWallet` cannot accidentally use some legacy wallet function. Additionally, `LegacyDataSPKM` is moved into a new file and this new namespace so that it cannot be used outside of migration.

Lastly, `ReorderTransactions` is a legacy wallet only function that is also moved into `LegacyWallet`.

Builds upon #34909, and depends on #36823 for removing some functions that were previously used by migration.

pulls.title: kernel: Dispatch log callbacks with btcsignals
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A kernel application whose log callback logs, or destroys a kernel object, hangs. The common way to hit this is a garbage-collected language binding: Python's garbage collector can run finalizers inside the callback, and a finalizer that destroys a chainstate manager flushes and logs (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34775#issuecomment-6278257737, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34374#discussion_r4030551866). The cause is that the kernel calls log callbacks while holding the logger's mutex, so any logging from inside a callback blocks on a mutex its own thread already holds. The problem is not new and has existed since logging callbacks were introduced in #30595.

**Solution:** This PR delivers log entries through `btcsignals::signal`, which calls callbacks without holding any lock, replacing the kernel's own callback list and custom dispatching mechanism.

The change is a usability improvement and a bugfix because with it applications no longer need to reason about deadlocks and blocking behavior from a mutex they can't see. However, they may need to be updated to deal with log callbacks that are no longer serialized and connection functions that no longer block. Compatibility details are in the commit message.

The main code change is in `src/kernel/bitcoinkernel.cpp` (+42/-77) accompanied by header docs and new test_kernel cases, which hang without the fix. There is also a commit switching `btcsignals.h` to use `StdMutex` instead of `Mutex` so it is safe to use in logging callbacks.

This is an alternative to the last commit of #34775, which fixes the same deadlock but only after limiting the process to one logging connection, and still hangs if a callback destroys the connection.

pulls.title: refactor : Reorder CBlockIndex members to save 8 bytes
pulls.body:
It seems we can save 8 bytes per CBlockIndex instance by reordering one class member. Moving one 8-byte field seems to avoid losing 2x 4 bytes to structure padding on a 64-bit build (on a 32-bit build, there is no gain).

I could not exactly measure the runtime gain from just this (smaller than RAM usage variation between 2 launches), but I confirmed there was about as many instances of CBlockIndex as blocks in the chain (increasing CBlockIndex size by 320 bytes increases RAM usage by ~300MB), so saving 8 bytes per instance should save about 8MB of RAM at current block height.

The gain is small, but it seems like it has no cost/risk, since that structure is not used for serialization, and just reordering here should have no side effects.

I saw a few other types that could gain a few bytes in size by doing something similar (for example, CTxIn), but they have far fewer instances in memory to make the change worth it.

pulls.title: wallet: fill PSBT_GLOBAL_XPUB
pulls.body:
Closes #27583.

`PSBT_GLOBAL_XPUB` already serializes, deserializes and merges when PSBTs are combined. Nothing writes it, so a PSBT produced by the wallet never carries it, and a signer that only has the file cannot rebuild the multisig from it. Today Specter [fills the field itself](https://github.com/cryptoadvance/specter-desktop/blob/8843e2f0640a9adc129f9ab6afe5ecb9632e7c5b/src/cryptoadvance/specter/wallet/wallet.py#L1866-L1881) after getting the PSBT from Core.

<details><summary>Before and after with the BitBox02 and Trezor simulators</summary>

A 2-of-3 `wsh(sortedmulti(...))` on regtest with the simulator as one co-signer, signed through HWI 3.2.0. The "before" file is the same PSBT with its `PSBT_GLOBAL_XPUB` records removed, so nothing else differs.

| | without the field | with the field |
|---|---|---|
| BitBox02 | refuses, `This BitBox02 is not one of the cosigners` | signs |
| Trezor T | signs, co-signer nodes sent with zeroed chain codes and no derivation paths | signs, nodes sent with the real chain codes and paths |

What `parse_multisig` hands the Trezor for the change output:

```
without: global xpubs=0  zeroed chain codes=3/3  depths=[0, 0, 0]  paths=[[], [], []]
with   : global xpubs=3  zeroed chain codes=0/3  depths=[4, 4, 4]  paths=[[1, 0], [1, 0], [1, 0]]
```

</details>

A new `Descriptor` accessor returns the extended keys a descriptor is built from, and `DescriptorScriptPubKeyMan::FillPSBT` writes those of every descriptor with an input or an output in the PSBT. That covers `walletcreatefundedpsbt`, `walletprocesspsbt`, `send`, `sendall`, `psbtbumpfee` and the GUI send dialog, which all go through `CWallet::FillPSBT`.

Only the keys BIP 174 allows are added, the ones that derive, through unhardened steps alone, a key their descriptor produced, listed in the PSBT at the origin the descriptor gave it. So a key expression ending in `/*h` adds nothing.

Whoever holds a PSBT from the wallet can now derive the addresses of the descriptors it uses. Setting `bip32derivs` to false in `walletcreatefundedpsbt` or `walletprocesspsbt` stops the wallet from adding the field, along with the derivation paths, and does not remove what a PSBT already carries.

`descriptorprocesspsbt` is left out, since it signs from the descriptors it is given without going through the wallet, and I intend to cover it as a follow-up.

pulls.title: bip352: match P2SH-P2WPKH instead of evaluating it
pulls.body:
For P2SH inputs, `GetPubKeyFromInput` evaluated the full scriptSig with `EvalScript` and then ran `Solver` on the redeem script, even though only P2SH-P2WPKH is eligible for BIP-352. That costs time on every non-segwit P2SH spend (e.g. multisig), whose scriptSigs can be up to `MAX_SCRIPT_SIZE`.

BIP-141 requires the scriptSig of a P2SH-wrapped witness program to be exactly a single push of the redeem script (`SCRIPT_ERR_WITNESS_MALLEATED_P2SH`). So any valid P2SH-P2WPKH scriptSig is exactly `0x16 OP_0 0x14 <20-byte keyhash>`, and matching that template gives the same result without evaluating anything.

### Benchmarks

`bench_bitcoin -filter='BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_.*' -min-time=2000`, Release build.

Before:

|            ns/input |             input/s |    err% |     total | benchmark
|--------------------:|--------------------:|--------:|----------:|:----------
|              688.30 |        1,452,858.07 |    0.1% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_Multisig`
|            7,158.19 |          139,700.11 |    0.1% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_P2WPKH`

After:

|            ns/input |             input/s |    err% |     total | benchmark
|--------------------:|--------------------:|--------:|----------:|:----------
|               56.87 |       17,584,611.40 |    0.0% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_Multisig`
|            6,949.45 |          143,896.18 |    0.0% |      2.20 | `BIP352_GetPubKey_P2SH_P2WPKH`

P2SH multisig is about 12x faster to rule out. P2SH-P2WPKH saves about 200 ns per input; its time is still dominated by `CPubKey::IsFullyValid()`.

pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: replace `loadtxoutset` RPC with a startup arg
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Loading a UTXO snapshot through RPC requires coordinating with the active chain, mempool, caches and advertised services while the node is running.

**Fix:** Replace the `loadtxoutset` RPC with `-loadtxoutset=<file>` and finish importing during chainstate initialization, before networking and mempool loading begin.
Require a receiver that has not advanced beyond genesis, already knows the snapshot base header and has no stored blocks beyond genesis or unfinished reindexing.
This removes runtime activation checks, temporary import cache resizing and service demotion while preserving snapshot validation, resumption and background validation.

pulls.title: util: Add and use AssertUnreachable
pulls.body:
The current code uses assertions with falsy literal values in a few places. This is perfectly fine, but this comes with a bit of confusion sometimes:

* `assert(false)` may cause confusion when it is unclear if `NDEBUG` can disable it. (The intention is to disallow `NDEBUG` compilation). Also, it can lead to warnings when used with clang-cl.exe (GCC seems to understand it)
* `Assert(false)` hides the noreturn attribute behind a function call, which may cause GCC return-type warnings. (Clang seems to understand it)

See https://godbolt.org/z/h7PT3jh3Y for the clang-cl/GCC warning reproducer.

* When C++23 will be allowed, devs may prefer `std::unreachable`. However, this is unsafe and will invoke UB.
* There is confusion why a `CHECK_NONFATAL` macro exists, but no fatal equivalent.

Fix all those issues by:

* Adding a new `AssertUnreachable`, which directly calls the noreturn `internal_abort_helper` helper.
* Adding an `assert_falsy` linter to enforce code to use this macro.
